title: Redeeming the firstborn
hook: a ceremony at thirty days for a firstborn son

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was simchat bat, and your line was welcome her. Which daughter heard the true thing you named? Today, a ceremony with a question in the middle of it. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

A father stands at a table, holding his month-old son. Across from him stands a kohen, a man from the priestly families. Between them, five silver coins. And the kohen asks a strange question, from a set script handed down for the ceremony. Which would you rather have: your firstborn son, or the five coins the Torah says you owe for him? The father, of course, chooses his son. He hands over the coins. The kohen takes them and blesses the child. Then everyone eats. Today's word is that exchange.
screen: `A FATHER, A KOHEN, FIVE COINS.` → `YOUR SON, OR THE SILVER?` → `HE CHOOSES HIS SON.`

segments.voice: Pidyon haben. Redemption of the son. Turn it four ways. First, the command. Exodus tells Israel to set apart every firstborn to God, and then says the firstborn sons are to be redeemed. Numbers gives the terms: from a month old, the redemption price is five shekels of silver, paid to the priests. So the ceremony waits until the baby has lived a month, and then the debt comes due. Second, the reason. Exodus ties it to the night of the Exodus, when the firstborn of Egypt died and the firstborn of Israel were spared. When your son asks what this means, the text says, you tell him: by strength of hand God brought us out. A firstborn son is a living reminder of a night when firstborns were saved. Third, the replacement. In Numbers, God takes the Levites in place of the firstborn, to serve at the sanctuary. The firstborn are released into ordinary life, and the silver marks the release. Not every family holds the ceremony: it is for a mother's firstborn when it is a son, and families of kohanim and Levites are exempt. Fourth, the blessing. When the coins change hands, the kohen often blesses the child with the priestly blessing from Numbers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." The question was never really about money. It's a way of saying, out loud, in front of witnesses: this child is a gift, and we know it.
screen: `FROM A MONTH OLD, FIVE SHEKELS.` · `SPARED ON THE NIGHT OF THE EXODUS.` · `THE LEVITES SERVE INSTEAD.` · `THE LORD BLESS THEE.` · then, large: `REDEMPTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about it, and let it land. Settle, and breathe. Bring the scene back: the table, the coins, the question. Your son, or the silver? Now turn the question toward your own life. Name one person you would never trade for anything, however the question is put. Hold their face for a few breaths. Then notice: when did you last tell them? If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Pidyon haben. Redemption of the firstborn son: a month old, five silver coins, a kohen's question and a blessing. Today's word.
Your line: redemption. Today, tell the person you named that you'd choose them, in your own plain words. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: When a mother's firstborn child is a son, many observant Jewish families hold a pidyon haben once he is a month old: the father gives a kohen five silver coins, blessings are said, and a festive meal follows.
